paragraphs: Going in to Lise, he found her half lying back in the invalid chair, the one she used to be wheeled around in when she couldn’t walk. She made no move to greet him. Her sharp, keen eyes simply stayed fastened on his face. There was a feverish look in them, and her face was pale and yellow. Alyosha was astonished at how she had changed in only three days. She had actually grown thinner. She did not offer him her hand. He touched her long, thin fingers where they lay motionless on her dress, and sat down opposite her without a word.
“I know you’re in a hurry to get to the prison,” Lise said shortly, “and Mamma has kept you there for hours, telling you about me and Yulia.”
“How do you know that?” asked Alyosha.
“I was listening. Why are you staring at me? I wanted to listen, so I did. What’s wrong with that? I won’t say sorry.”
“Has something upset you?”

“Quite the opposite, I’m very happy. For the thirtieth time I’ve just been thinking how lucky it is that I refused you and won’t be your wife. You’d make a hopeless husband. Say I married you, and then handed you a note for the man I loved after you. You’d take it, you’d certainly deliver it, and you’d bring his answer back, too. You could be forty and you’d still be running my love letters for me.”
Suddenly she laughed.
“You’re spiteful, and yet you’re open-hearted, too,” Alyosha said to her, smiling.

“The open-hearted part is that I’m not ashamed of myself in front of you. More than that, I don’t want to be ashamed in front of you, only you. Alyosha, why don’t I respect you? I’m very fond of you, but I don’t respect you. If I did, I couldn’t talk to you so shamelessly, could I?”
“No.”
“But do you believe I feel no shame with you?”
“No, I don’t believe that.”
Again Lise gave a nervous laugh, and she began to speak fast.
“I sent your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch some sweets in prison. You know, Alyosha, you’re rather pretty! I’m going to love you terribly for letting me stop loving you so quickly.”
“Why did you send for me today, Lise?”
“I wanted to tell you something I long for. I’d like somebody to torture me. To marry me and then torture me, to deceive me and leave. I don’t want to be happy.”
“You’re in love with chaos?”

“Yes, I want chaos. I keep wanting to burn the house down. I keep picturing how I’d creep up and set it alight on the sly. It has to be on the sly. They’d try to put it out, but it would keep burning. And I’d know, and say nothing. Ah, how silly! And how bored I am!”
She waved a hand, looking disgusted.
“It’s the soft life you lead,” Alyosha said gently.
“So being poor is better?”
“Yes, it is better.”

“That’s what your monk has taught you. It isn’t true. Let me be rich and everybody else poor. I’d eat sweets and drink cream and share with nobody. Ach, don’t talk, don’t say a word,” she shook her hand at him, though Alyosha hadn’t opened his mouth. “You’ve told me all this before. I know it by heart. It bores me. If I’m ever poor, I’ll murder someone, and if I’m rich, I might murder someone anyway, why just sit there? But do you know, I’d like to go reaping, to cut rye? I’ll marry you and you’ll turn into a peasant, a proper peasant. We’ll keep a colt, shall we? Do you know Kalganov?”
“Yes.”

“He’s forever drifting about, daydreaming. He says, ‘Why live in real life? Dreaming is better. You can dream up the loveliest things, but real life is a bore.’ And yet he’ll be married soon enough. He’s already been courting me. Can you spin a top?”
“Yes.”

“Well, he’s exactly like a top. He needs winding up and setting spinning, and then lashing, lashing, lashing with a whip. If I marry him, I’ll keep him spinning his whole life. You’re not ashamed to be with me?”
“No.”
“You’re terribly cross with me because I don’t talk about holy things. I don’t want to be holy. What do they do to you in the next world for the very worst sin? You ought to know all about that.”
“God will condemn you.” Alyosha watched her steadily.
“That’s just what I’d like. I’d walk up, they’d condemn me, and I’d burst out laughing in their faces. I’d dearly love to burn the house down, Alyosha, our house. You still don’t believe me?”
“Why wouldn’t I? There are children of twelve years old who long to set fire to something, and they really do set things on fire, too. It’s a kind of sickness.”
“That isn’t true, it isn’t! There may be children like that, but that’s not what I mean.”
“You mistake evil for good. It’s a crisis that will pass. Maybe it comes from your illness.”
“So you do despise me! It’s just that I don’t want to do good, I want to do evil. It has nothing to do with illness.”
“Why do evil?”

“So that everything would be destroyed. Ah, how lovely it would be if everything were destroyed! You know, Alyosha, sometimes I think of doing a terrible amount of harm, every bad thing there is. I’d keep doing it quietly for a long time, and then suddenly everybody would find out. They’d all stand around pointing at me, and I’d look back at them. That would be awfully nice. Why would it be so nice, Alyosha?”
“I don’t know. It’s a craving to wreck something good or, as you put it, to set something on fire. It happens at times.”
“I’m not only saying it, I’ll do it.”
“I believe you.”
“Ah, how I love you for saying you believe me. And you’re not lying even a little. But maybe you think I’m saying all this deliberately, to annoy you?”
“No, I don’t think so... although maybe there is a small wish to annoy me in it.”
“A small one, yes. I can never lie to you,” she declared, with a strange fire in her eyes.

What struck Alyosha most of all was how earnest she was. Not a trace of humor or teasing showed in her face now, though in the old days her fun and gaiety never left her, even at her most “earnest” moments.
“There are moments when people love crime,” Alyosha said thoughtfully.

“Yes, yes! You’ve put my own thought into words. They love crime, everybody loves crime, and always, not just at some ‘moments.’ It’s as if people had agreed together to lie about it, and have been lying ever since. They all say they hate evil, but in secret they all love it.”
“And are you still reading those nasty books?”
“Yes. Mamma reads them and hides them under her pillow, and I steal them.”
“Aren’t you ashamed, ruining yourself like that?”

“I want to ruin myself. There’s a boy here who lay down between the railway lines while a train went over. Lucky fellow! Listen, your brother is on trial now for killing his father, and everybody loves the fact that he killed his father.”
“Loves the fact that he killed his father?”
“Yes, loves it! Everybody does! They all say it’s so dreadful, but secretly they just love it. I, for one, love it.”
“There’s some truth in what you say about everybody,” Alyosha said softly.

“Oh, the ideas you have!” Lise shrieked with delight. “And you a monk! You can’t think how much I respect you, Alyosha, for never telling lies. Oh, I must tell you a funny dream I have. Sometimes I dream of devils. It’s night, I’m in my room with a candle, and suddenly devils are everywhere, in every corner, under the table. They open the doors, and a crowd of them stands behind the doors, wanting to come in and grab me. They’re just coming, just grabbing me. But suddenly I make the sign of the cross, and they all shrink back, though they don’t leave altogether. They wait at the doors and in the corners. Then a terrible longing comes over me to curse God out loud, and so I start, and they come crowding back, delighted, and grab me again. I cross myself again and they all shrink back. It’s awful fun. It takes your breath away.”
“I’ve had that same dream,” said Alyosha suddenly.
“Have you really?” cried Lise, surprised. “Listen, Alyosha, don’t laugh, this is terribly important. Can two different people have the same dream?”
“Apparently they can.”

“Alyosha, I’m telling you, it’s terribly important,” Lise went on, with truly excessive astonishment. “The dream isn’t what matters. What matters is that you had the same dream as me. You never lie to me, so don’t lie now. Is it true? You’re not laughing at me?”
“It’s true.”
Lise seemed extraordinarily struck, and for half a minute she said nothing.
“Alyosha, come and see me, come more often,” she said suddenly, in a begging voice.
“I’ll come to see you all my life,” Alyosha answered firmly.

“You’re the only person I can talk to, you know,” Lise began again. “I talk to nobody except myself and you. You alone in the whole world. And I talk to you more easily than to myself. And I’m not at all ashamed with you, not at all. Alyosha, why am I not ashamed with you, not at all? Alyosha, is it true that at Easter the Jews steal a child and kill it?”
“I don’t know.”

“There’s a book here where I read about the trial of a Jew. He took a child of four years old and cut the fingers off both hands. Then he crucified him on a wall, hammered nails into him and crucified him, and afterwards, at his trial, he said the child had died soon, within four hours. ‘Soon,’ he called that! He said the child moaned and went on moaning, and he stood there admiring it. That’s nice!”
“Nice?”
“Yes, nice. Sometimes I imagine I’m the one who crucified him. He hangs there moaning, and I sit across from him eating pineapple _compote_. I’m awfully fond of pineapple _compote_. Are you?”
Alyosha looked at her without speaking. Her pale, sallow face suddenly twisted, and her eyes burned.

“You know, after I read about that Jew, I sobbed and shook the whole night. I kept imagining how the poor little thing cried and moaned (a child of four understands, you know), and all the time I couldn’t get the pineapple _compote_ out of my head. In the morning I wrote a letter to a certain person, begging him _especially_ to come and see me. He came, and I suddenly told him everything about the child and the pineapple _compote_. _Everything_, _everything_, and I said it was nice. He laughed and said it really was nice. Then he got up and left. He was here only five minutes. Did he despise me? Did he despise me? Tell me, tell me, Alyosha, did he despise me or not?” She sat up on the couch, her eyes flashing.
“Tell me,” Alyosha asked anxiously, “was it you who sent for that person?”
“Yes, me.”
“You sent him a letter?”
“Yes.”
“Only to ask about that, about that child?”
“No, nothing to do with that. But as soon as he arrived, I asked him about it. He answered me, laughed, stood up and left.”
“That person behaved honorably,” Alyosha murmured.
“And did he despise me? Did he laugh at me?”
“No, because maybe he believes in the pineapple _compote_ himself. He’s very ill just now, too, Lise.”
“Yes, he does believe in it,” said Lise, her eyes flashing.
“He despises nobody,” Alyosha went on. “It’s only that he believes nobody. And if he doesn’t believe in people, then of course he does despise them.”
“So he despises me, me?”
“You, too.”
“Good,” said Lise, as if grinding her teeth. “When he walked out laughing, I felt that being despised was nice. The child with his fingers cut off is nice, and being despised is nice...”
And she laughed in Alyosha’s face, a feverish, spiteful laugh.

“Do you know, Alyosha, do you know, I’d like—Alyosha, save me!” She suddenly leaped from the couch, rushed at him and grabbed him with both hands. “Save me!” she almost groaned. “Is there anyone in the world I could tell what I’ve told you? I’ve told you the truth, the truth. I’m going to kill myself, because I loathe everything! I don’t want to live, because I loathe everything! I loathe everything, everything. Alyosha, why don’t you love me even a little?” she ended in a frenzy.
“But I do love you!” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And will you weep for me, will you?”
“Yes.”
“Not because I won’t be your wife, but just weep for me?”
“Yes.”

“Thank you! Your tears are all I want. Let everyone else punish me and trample me underfoot, everyone, everyone, _anyone_ at all. Because I don’t love anyone. Do you hear, not anyone! On the contrary, I hate him! Go, Alyosha. It’s time you went to your brother”; and she suddenly tore herself away from him.
“How can I leave you like this?” said Alyosha, almost alarmed.
“Go to your brother, the prison will close. Go, here’s your hat. Give Mitya my love, go, go!”

And she almost forced Alyosha out the door by pushing him. He looked at her in pained surprise, and then he noticed a letter in his right hand, a tiny letter folded tight and sealed. He glanced at it and read the address at once: “To Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov.” He looked quickly at Lise. Her face had turned almost threatening.
“Give it to him, you must give it to him!” she ordered, trembling and beside herself. “Today, right now, or I’ll poison myself! That’s why I sent for you.”

And she slammed the door at once. The bolt clicked. Alyosha put the note in his pocket and went straight downstairs without returning to Madame Hohlakov. In fact, he forgot her. As soon as he had gone, Lise unbolted the door, opened it a crack, stuck her finger in the gap and slammed the door with all her strength, crushing her finger. Ten seconds later she pulled her finger free, walked slowly and softly back to her chair, sat bolt upright in it, and stared hard at her blackened finger and at the blood seeping out from under the nail. Her lips were trembling, and she kept whispering rapidly to herself:
“I’m a wretch, wretch, wretch, wretch!”
